title: Why "When Will This Ship?" Is a Trap for PMs
description:
A sales lead puts you on the spot in an all-hands: "Will SSO be ready by our renewal date?" The wrong answer turns your roadmap into a broken promise. This Short breaks down the Now/Next/Later confidence structure and the exact line a PM uses to answer honestly without over-committing.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/product-manager-mastery-path/level-1/08-roadmapping-basics/

#Shorts

beats.narration: Picture this: you're in an all-hands, and a sales lead puts you on the spot. "Will SSO be ready by our renewal date?" The room goes quiet.

display.heading: The Question That Puts PMs On The Spot

beats.narration: Your roadmap only labels this a Next theme -- a likely priority, but no firm date yet. Now is locked in. Later is just a directional bet.

display.heading: Now / Next / Later
display.subheading: Now: named, mostly locked. Next: themes, no firm dates. Later: directional only, subject to change.

beats.narration: Here's the trap: every stakeholder will eventually try to hold a roadmap item to its literal wording as a promise.

display.heading: A roadmap is a communication tool, not a contract
display.subheading: Stating the confidence level out loud, every time, heads this off before it becomes a trust problem later.

beats.narration: The right answer: "That's a Next-horizon theme, not a committed item. I can flag your timeline need, but I can't commit a date today."

display.heading: The PM's actual line
display.subheading: "I can flag your specific timeline need to prioritization, but I can't commit a date today."

beats.narration: It's a harder thing to say live than a vague "probably." But it's what keeps your roadmap trustworthy the next time you share it.

display.heading: Harder to say. Worth it.
display.subheading: Trust compounds -- or erodes -- one roadmap conversation at a time.
